unit.title: Mark off/out structural fabrication and shapes

summary: This unit teaches you to mark out steel accurately for fabrication: plate, structural sections such as angle, channel and beams, and pipe. You will learn to plan the job from the drawing, use and care for marking-out tools, work from datums, use simple geometry for right angles, circles and hole patterns, mark holes, cut lines, mitres and copes, make templates and simple pattern developments, allow for the kerf, bending and shrinkage, and check your work before anything is cut.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 2 qualification (MEM22423). **Marking out** (also called marking off or setting out) means transferring the sizes and shapes on a drawing onto the steel, as lines, centre marks and labels, so that the parts can be cut, drilled, bent and fitted. Every later step depends on it. A part marked wrongly is cut wrongly, and steel that has been cut too short cannot be put back.

In Jamaican fabrication shops you will mark out base plates, brackets and gussets, columns and beams for roofs and mezzanines, frames for gates, grilles and water-tank stands, and pipe for handrails, pump houses and irrigation. The skills are the same on a small job and a large one: work from a datum, measure carefully, mark clearly and check before you cut.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 2 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and anyone who prepares steel for cutting, drilling and welding. You should already be able to read a simple drawing and use a tape measure.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Plan the marking-out job
Read the drawing and job card, check that the sizes add up, make or check a cutting list, check the material, choose datums and plan the allowances.
Work safely
Lift and support steel safely, protect your hands and eyes, and look after sharp tools and marking fluids.
Use and care for marking-out tools
Choose the right tool and marker for the surface and the job, use it correctly, and keep it accurate.
Work from datums and check accuracy
Measure every size from a datum, check squareness with diagonals or the 3-4-5 rule, and avoid errors that add up.
Use geometry
Mark right angles, parallel lines, arcs, circles, centres and equal divisions of a circle.
Mark holes
Mark hole centres from the pitch, end distance, edge distance, back mark and pitch circle, then punch them and add witness marks.
Mark sections and pipe
Carry square lines round angle, channel, beams and pipe; mark mitres, copes and notches; find the quarter lines on a pipe.
Make templates and developments
Make, check and label templates; develop simple shapes such as a pipe mitre and a cone frustum.
Allow, check and identify
Allow for the kerf, bending, machining and weld shrinkage; check the job before it is cut; mark part numbers; report problems.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on planning, safety, tools, datums, geometry, holes, sections, pipe, templates, development, allowances and checking.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact trade words such as plumb bob, end distance, cope, apex and parallax, and simple sums) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: marking out a base plate with bolt holes on a rectangle and on a pitch circle, and developing a paper template for a 90° two-piece pipe mitre and marking it onto pipe. The assessor watches how you work (datums, checking, safe handling, tool care), not only the finished marks.

blocks.note: Many questions are sums: diagonals, circumferences, hole positions and the spacing of holes on a circle. Practise them with a calculator until they are quick, and always write the unit (mm) with your answer.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Read the drawing and the job card

ul: Check that the **drawing number and revision** match the job card. An old revision may have different sizes.
Read the title block (title, scale, units, material, projection), every view, the sizes, the hole details and the notes.
Check that the sizes **add up**: the sizes along a line should add up to the overall size given.
**Never measure a size off the drawing paper.** Paper stretches and prints are rarely exactly to scale. If a size is missing or does not add up, stop and ask your supervisor.
Note how many of each part are needed, and whether any are **opposite hand** (a left-hand and a right-hand version).

blocks.p: A **cutting list** sets out every part: its part mark, the section and size, the length, the quantity and any notes. Make it, or check the one you are given, before you mark anything. It lets you plan the cuts from stock lengths with the least waste.

blocks.p: Steel is usually sold in **6 m lengths** (about 20 ft). Five 1 200 mm legs cannot be cut from one 6 m length: 5 × 1 200 = 6 000 mm, but each of the four cuts removes a few millimetres, so the last leg comes out short. Plan four legs from each length and use the rest for shorter parts.

ul: Right section and size: measure the legs, flange widths, thickness or diameter with a tape and a vernier caliper.
Straight and not twisted: sight along it, or check it against a string line or a straight edge.
Sound: no deep rust or pitting, cracks, laminations (layers splitting apart at a cut edge), dents or bends.
Long enough for the parts on the cutting list, with allowances.
The right material: check the label, the colour code or the supplier's certificate. If you are not sure, set it aside and ask.

blocks.note: Steel in Jamaica comes from several countries, so suppliers and drawings may give sizes in millimetres or in inches (1 inch = 25.4 mm), and sheet thickness may be given as a gauge number. Check what the drawing really asks for and convert carefully: "2 in" angle is about 50.8 mm, not 50 mm.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Read the drawing and the job card
Make or check the cutting list
Check the material
Choose the datums
Note the allowances: kerf, bends, machining, weld shrinkage
Collect and check the tools
Set the steel up safely at a good working height
Mark, check, then punch and label

head: Hazard
What can happen
How you control it
rows: Heavy plate and sections
Crushed hands and feet, back injury, steel rolling or tipping off the trestles
Enough people or a lifting aid for the weight
Safety boots
Firm trestles at working height
Round bar, pipe and channel chocked so they cannot roll
Sharp edges and burrs
Deep cuts to the hands and arms
Gloves when handling
Burrs filed or ground off
Never slide a bare hand along a cut edge
Punching and hammering
Chips of steel, or the burr from a mushroomed punch head, fly into the eyes
Safety glasses
Mushroomed heads ground off
A hammer with a tight head and a sound handle
Sharp points
Scriber, divider and trammel points stab hands and legs
Points covered when not in use
Carried pointing down, never in a pocket
Tape measures
The blade snaps back and cuts the fingers
Let it run back slowly under control
Marking fluids and paint markers
Fumes in a closed space; many are flammable
Good ventilation
Caps on
Kept away from sparks and flames
Trips
Offcuts, steel and tools left on the floor
Floor kept clear; offcuts in racks or bins
Hot steel
Plate just cut or welded looks the same as cold plate
Mark it HOT with soapstone
Move it with tongs or let it cool

blocks.note: When two or more people lift a long section, agree who gives the commands, then lift, carry and put down together. Never stand under a load that is being lifted, and never use your hands to stop a swinging section.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Much marking out is done in the yard in full sun. Steel in the sun can get hot enough to burn, and it grows as it warms: a 6 m bar that warms by 30 °C gets about 2 mm longer. On long, accurate work, mark and check at the same time of day, and drink water often.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Good marking out needs the right tool for each job, used correctly and kept accurate. A damaged tool gives wrong marks however carefully you work.

head: Tool
What it is used for
How to keep it accurate
rows: Steel rule (300 mm to 1 m)
Short measurements; a straight edge for scribing short lines
Keep the edges and the zero end free of dents and wear; never use it as a scraper, screwdriver or lever; wipe and oil it lightly.
Tape measure (3–8 m) and long tape (up to 30 m)
Long measurements on plate and sections

Check that the hook is not bent or loose. It is meant to slide by its own thickness, so that inside and outside readings are both right. Compare the tape with a steel rule now and then, and replace a kinked or worn blade.
Engineer's square
Marking and checking lines at 90° to a straight edge
Do not drop it; keep the stock pressed against the edge; check it now and then against a known square.
Combination set
One rule with three heads: a square head (90° and 45°), a protractor head (any angle) and a centre head (the centre of a round bar)
Keep the heads clean and the locking screws working; do not drop it.
Framing (steel) square
Large right angles on plate and frames
Store it flat or hung up; check it against a known right angle.
Straight edge
Long straight lines; checking that an edge or surface is straight
Store it flat or hung so that it does not bend.
Spirit level
Checking level and plumb on frames and columns
Check it by turning it end for end on a flat surface: the bubble should read the same.
Plumb bob
A true vertical line, for example when setting out columns and posts
Keep the string untangled and the point undamaged.
Vernier caliper
Thickness, outside diameter and small sizes, read to a fraction of a millimetre
Check that it reads zero with the jaws closed; keep it clean and in its case.

head: Tool
What it is used for
Care
rows: Scriber
Fine, lasting lines on clean or blued metal
Keep the point sharp and covered.
Soapstone (French chalk)
Lines on rough, rusty or hot plate, and lines for flame cutting; it does not burn off in the heat
Sharpen it to a chisel edge for a fine line.
Paint marker
Part marks, job numbers and lines that must last through handling and weather
Cap it after use; shake it before use.
Marking blue (layout fluid)
A thin coat on clean, bright metal so that scribed lines show up clearly
Cap it; use it with good ventilation, away from flames.
Chalk line
Long straight lines across large plates and long sections
Keep the line dry and clean; pull it tight before you snap it.
Dot (prick) punch
Light dots at a centre or along a line, so that the mark survives handling
Keep the fine point sharp (often ground to about 60°).
Centre punch
A bigger dent at a hole centre so that the drill starts in the right place
Keep the point at about 90°; grind off a mushroomed head.
Ball-pein hammer
Striking punches
Head tight; handle sound.
Dividers
Small circles and arcs; stepping off equal distances
Points sharp and of equal length; joint firm so that it does not slip.
Trammels (beam compass)
Large arcs and circles, too big for dividers
Heads tight on the beam; points sharp.
Odd-leg (jenny) calipers
Lines parallel to an edge; finding the centre of a bar
Keep the point sharp and the joint firm.
Centre head or centre finder
The centre of the end of a round bar or pipe
Keep the V clean and undamaged.
Wraparound (flexible strip)
Square lines round a pipe
Keep it flat and clean; replace it when it is kinked.
Templates
Repeat shapes and hole patterns
Check against the drawing; label; store flat.

blocks.note: Use the dot punch first: tap lightly, check the position, and only then enlarge the correct dots with the centre punch. A light dot that is in the wrong place can be ignored; a deep centre punch mark will pull the drill to the wrong place.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Surface or job
Best marker
Why
rows: Clean, bright or machined metal; accurate work
Marking blue and a scriber
A fine, sharp line that shows clearly
Rusty, mill-scaled or rough plate
Soapstone, or a scribed line on a cleaned strip
Shows on dark surfaces; loose scale flakes off and takes the marks with it, so clean where accuracy matters
Lines that will be flame or plasma cut
Soapstone, with punch dots along the line
Soapstone stands the heat; the dots still show after the cut
Part marks and job numbers
Paint marker
Lasts through handling, weather and storage
Long lines on large plates
Chalk line, then scribe or punch along it
Quick and straight over long distances
Bend lines on aluminium, coated or thin sheet
A fine marker, not a deep scribed line
A scratch where the metal bends can start a crack, and it breaks the coating

blocks.note: Keep lines fine. A blunt soapstone line can be 2 mm wide, which is a large error on accurate work. Sharpen soapstone to a chisel edge, and scribe on marking blue when accuracy matters.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **datum** is the line, edge, face or point that all the measurements are taken from. On a plate it is usually two straight, square edges at one corner. On a section it may be one end and the back of the web or the back of an angle. On a symmetrical part it may be a centre line.

If you measure each size from the last mark (**chain measuring**), every small error is carried on to the next mark, and the errors add up. Suppose you mark ten holes at 80 mm pitch and each step is 0.5 mm too long. There are nine steps, so the last hole is 4.5 mm out. If you measure every hole from the datum (35 mm, 115 mm, 195 mm and so on), each hole is only as wrong as one reading.

head: Method
How it works
Result
rows: Chain measuring (mark to mark)
Each size measured from the mark before
Errors add up along the job; one wrong mark moves all the marks after it
Datum measuring
Every size measured from the same datum
Errors do not add up; each mark can be checked on its own

blocks.note: Before you start, write the running figures from the datum on your sketch or job card (for example 35, 115, 195, 275). Then hook the tape on the datum once and mark every point without moving it.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Check that the edge is **straight** with a straight edge or a tight string line.
Check that the two datum edges are **square** to each other with an engineer's square or a framing square.
Sheared and flame-cut edges are often not straight or square. If an edge is not good enough, scribe a datum line a little way in from it and work from the line instead.
Mark the datum edges clearly (for example with a paint mark or the letters DATUM) so that everyone works from the same edges.
Look **straight down** at the graduation when you mark. Looking from the side moves the mark; this is called **parallax** error.
Stand the steel rule on its edge, so the graduations touch the metal.
If the end of a rule is worn, measure from the 10 mm line and take 10 mm off the reading.
Hold the tape tight and straight, and do not let it sag over a long distance.
Make a fine tick or a short scribed line exactly at the graduation, then square or scribe the full line through it.
Read the figures twice, especially 6 and 9, and centimetre and millimetre lines.
Work in millimetres: 1 m = 1 000 mm, so 2.4 m = 2 400 mm and 0.75 m = 750 mm. Writing every size in millimetres avoids mixing units.

blocks.p: In a true rectangle the two **diagonals are equal**. If they are not equal, the corners are not 90°. You can work out what each diagonal should be with Pythagoras: diagonal = √(length² + width²).

Example: a frame 1 500 mm × 800 mm. Diagonal = √(1 500² + 800²) = √(2 250 000 + 640 000) = √2 890 000 = **1 700 mm**. Measure both diagonals; if one is 1 706 mm and the other 1 694 mm, the frame is out of square. Push the two corners at the ends of the longer diagonal towards each other until both read 1 700 mm.

A triangle with sides of 3, 4 and 5 units has a right angle between the 3 and the 4 sides. Any multiple works: 300-400-500 mm, 600-800-1 000 mm, 1.2-1.6-2.0 m or 3-4-5 m. **The bigger the triangle, the more accurate the right angle.**

flow: Mark the corner point on the base line
Measure 3 units along the base line from the corner and mark it
Measure roughly 4 units up the line you want to set square, and mark it
Measure between the two marks and move the second mark until the distance is exactly 5 units
Draw or snap the line through the corner and the second mark

blocks.note: Pythagoras works with any sizes: for sides of 1 200 mm and 500 mm, the long side is √(1 200² + 500²) = √1 690 000 = 1 300 mm. Use whatever numbers suit the space you have.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **tolerance** is how far a size may be from the drawing and still be accepted. Drawings for general fabrication often allow about ±1 mm or ±2 mm, and closer limits on bolt holes that must line up with other parts. Follow the tolerance on the drawing; if none is given, ask what the shop's standard is.

head: Cause
How to avoid it
rows: Measuring from mark to mark, so errors add up
Measure every size from one datum
A datum edge that is not straight or square
Check the edge first; scribe a datum line if needed
Faulty tools: a bent or loose tape hook, a worn rule, a dropped square
Check tools before use; take damaged ones out of use and report them
Parallax: reading the rule from the side
Look straight down at the mark
Thick or unclear lines
Fine scribed lines on clean or blued metal; sharp soapstone on rough plate
Misreading the drawing or using an old revision
Check the drawing number and revision; ask when something is unclear
Forgetting allowances
List the kerf, bend, machining and shrinkage allowances before you start
Not checking
Re-measure from the datum, check the diagonals, and have the job checked before it is cut

blocks.p: Marking out uses a few simple geometric methods again and again. Learn them on paper with a compass, then on steel with dividers and trammels.

head: Word
Meaning
rows: Centre line
A line through the middle of a symmetrical part or a hole; also called a line of symmetry
Perpendicular
At 90° to another line
Parallel
The same distance apart all the way along
Bisect
Cut exactly in half
Radius and diameter
Centre to edge of a circle, and right across it through the centre (diameter = 2 × radius)
Circumference
The distance all the way round a circle
Chord
A straight line joining two points on a circle
Arc
Part of the curved edge of a circle
Pitch circle diameter (PCD)
The diameter of the circle on which the centres of a ring of holes lie
Angles of a triangle
The three inside angles of any triangle add up to 180°

blocks.h: A line at 90° from a point on an edge

flow: From the point, strike two small arcs that cut the edge at equal distances on each side
Open the dividers or trammels wider
From each of those two marks, strike an arc above the edge so that the arcs cross
Join the crossing point to the first point: this line is at 90° to the edge

blocks.h: Bisecting a line (finding its middle at 90°)

flow: Set the dividers or trammels to more than half the length of the line
From one end, strike arcs above and below the line
From the other end, with the same setting, strike arcs that cross the first two
Join the two crossing points: this line cuts the first line in half, at 90°

ul: **Parallel line:** set odd-leg calipers or a combination square to the distance and run it along the datum edge; or measure the same distance at both ends of the edge, as far apart as possible, and join the marks.
**Bisecting an angle:** from the corner, strike an arc that cuts both arms; from those two points strike equal arcs that cross; join the crossing to the corner.
**Centre of a circle or an arc:** draw two chords and bisect each one. The two bisecting lines cross at the centre.

**Centre of a round bar:** use the centre head of a combination set to draw two lines across the end at about 90° to each other; they cross at the centre. Odd-leg calipers set to about the radius, used from four sides, also find it.

blocks.p: Circumference = **π × diameter** (π is about 3.142). A circle 300 mm across is about 3.142 × 300 = 942.6 mm round. Turned the other way, diameter = circumference ÷ π: if a tape wrapped round a pipe reads 359 mm, the pipe is about 359 ÷ 3.142 = 114.3 mm across.

blocks.h: Dividing a circle into equal parts

blocks.p: For holes evenly spaced on a pitch circle, the angle between neighbouring holes is **360° ÷ the number of holes**. You can set this out with the protractor head, but on the job it is usually more accurate to step off the **chord** (the straight distance between neighbouring hole centres) with dividers or trammels. Chord = PCD × the factor in the table.

head: Number of holes
Angle between holes
Chord factor (× PCD)
Chord on a 240 mm PCD
rows: 0.500 (the radius)

blocks.note: The chord is a straight line, so it is shorter than the arc between the same two points. Do **not** set your dividers to the circumference divided by the number of holes: that is the arc length, and the last step will overshoot the first hole.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Marking holes on a pitch circle

flow: Scribe the two centre lines at 90° and lightly dot punch the centre
Scribe the pitch circle with dividers or trammels set to the radius (half the PCD)
Check on the drawing whether the holes sit on the centre lines or between them (for example four holes at 45°)
Set the dividers to the chord and step round the circle from the starting hole
The last step must land exactly on the first mark; if it does not, adjust the dividers a fraction and step round again
Dot punch the hole centres and check the chord between every pair
Centre punch, scribe the hole circles and add witness marks

blocks.note: Any error is spread over all the steps. If the last step lands 2.4 mm past the first mark on a ring of 12 holes, each step is about 0.2 mm too long: close the dividers by that much and step round again.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Hole centre
The point where the hole's centre lines cross; the drill point goes here
Pitch
The centre-to-centre distance between holes in a line
End distance
From the end of a member to the centre of the first hole
Edge distance
From the side edge of a plate or flange to the centre of a hole
Gauge
The distance between two lines of holes across a member
Back mark (gauge line)
On an angle or a channel flange, the distance from the back of the section to the line of holes
Pitch circle diameter (PCD)
The diameter of the circle through the centres of a ring of holes
Witness marks
A scribed circle (and often a few punch dots on it) round a hole centre, used to check the hole after drilling

blocks.p: Drawings describe holes with short notes. **4 × Ø18** means four holes, each 18 mm in diameter. **6 × Ø14 EQ SP ON 150 PCD** means six 14 mm holes equally spaced on a 150 mm pitch circle. Holes are usually a little bigger than the bolt that goes through them; the drawing gives the hole size, so mark that size.

blocks.h: Working out hole positions in a row

blocks.p: Position of the last hole from the datum end = **end distance + (number of holes − 1) × pitch**. For example, an end distance of 35 mm and six holes at 60 mm pitch: 35 + 5 × 60 = 335 mm. Mark every hole from the datum end: 35, 95, 155, 215, 275 and 335 mm.

Example: a plate 400 mm × 300 mm with four holes whose centres are 50 mm in from each edge. The hole centres are 400 − 100 = 300 mm apart along the length and 300 − 100 = 200 mm apart across the width.

flow: Check the plate size, and choose two straight, square edges at one corner as the datums; mark them
Clean the surface where you will mark and coat it thinly with marking blue
Check the outline: both diagonals should be √(400² + 300²) = 500 mm
From the long datum edge, scribe hole lines at 50 mm and 250 mm; from the short datum edge, scribe lines at 50 mm and 350 mm
Check the spacing (300 mm and 200 mm) and the diagonals between the hole centres: √(300² + 200²) ≈ 360.6 mm, both the same
Dot punch lightly where the lines cross, and check again
Centre punch the correct dots; scribe each hole circle with dividers set to half the hole size; add witness marks
Mark the job number and part mark with a paint marker

ul: Hold the punch upright, with its point exactly on the crossing of the lines. Tilt it to find the line, then stand it up before you strike.
Strike the dot punch lightly; strike the centre punch once, firmly. A second blow on a punch that has moved makes a double mark.
Make the centre punch dent big enough to hold the point of the drill (or the pilot drill) the shop will use.
Along a line that will be flame or plasma cut, punch dots evenly along it, closer together on curves, so the line can still be followed and checked after cutting.
Never punch hardened steel: the punch will not mark it and chips can fly.

blocks.p: Scribe a circle the size of the hole round each centre, and add a few small punch dots on the circle, or a second, larger circle. After drilling, a hole in the right place cuts through the witness circle evenly all round. If the hole has wandered, the witness mark shows more on one side than the other, so the error can be seen and put right before the part is fitted.

ul: On an **angle**, the back mark is measured from the **back (heel)** of the angle, the outside corner, across the leg. Do not measure from the toe (the free edge): the leg width and the rolled edge vary.
On a **channel**, the back mark for flange holes is measured from the back of the web. Holes in the web are set out from the face or line the drawing gives.
Standard back marks for each leg size are listed in steel section tables; use the figure on the drawing.
Mark the hole positions along a section from the **same datum end** you used for its length, so that the holes line up with the parts they bolt to.

blocks.note: Hammering and punching on a section that is not firmly supported makes it bounce and the punch slip. Support the section on firm trestles under the point you are punching, and chock round sections.
blocks.label: Safety

Shape

Example

50 × 8 flat

Diameter
Ø16 round bar

Solid square

12 mm square bar

Depth × flange width × mass per metre
Rectangular hollow section (RHS)

60.3 × 3.9 CHS (2 in schedule 40 pipe)

blocks.p: In a beam or column size, the last figure is the **mass per metre**. A UB 203 × 133 × 25 is about 203 mm deep and 133 mm wide, and weighs about 25 kg for every metre of length, so a 4 m length weighs about 100 kg. Use this to plan the lift.

blocks.note: Beams from the United States are named differently. W8 × 15 is a wide-flange beam about 8 inches deep that weighs 15 pounds per foot; C6 × 8.2 is a channel about 6 inches deep, 8.2 pounds per foot. Read the size on the drawing and on the label, and ask if they do not match.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: **Flange:** the wide, flat parts at the top and bottom of a beam or channel.
**Web:** the upright plate joining the flanges.
**Leg, heel and toe** of an angle: each side is a leg; the outside corner is the heel (back); the free edge of a leg is the toe.

**Root radius:** the curve on the inside corner where the web meets a flange, or the legs of an angle meet. A square placed in the inside corner will not sit tight, so mark from the outside (back) faces.

blocks.h: Marking a square cut line round a section

flow: Choose a datum face, for example the back of the web or the back of one leg
Measure the length along that face from the datum end
Square the line across the datum face
Carry the line round onto each other face, squaring each time from a face the line already crosses
Check that the lines meet where they come together; if they do not, check your square and the faces
Mark the waste side of the line with cross-hatching or an X

blocks.note: Rolled sections are not perfect: flanges may be slightly out of square with the web, and the ends supplied from the mill are not always square. Never take the mill end as your datum without checking it.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Cut
What it is
Marking points
rows: Mitre
Two members cut at matching angles so that they meet at a corner
The joint line halves the corner angle: a 90° corner needs a 45° cut on each piece
A six-sided frame has 120° corners, so the joint line is at 60° to each bar
Mark both pieces of a corner as a pair, and check which face the length is measured on (inside or outside)
Cope
The end of a beam shaped to fit round the flange of the beam it joins
Mark the depth and length of the cut-out from the drawing, measured from the top of the flange and the end
The inside corner is rounded (often by drilling a hole first) so that the cut has no sharp corner that could crack
Mark the waste side
Notch
A piece cut out of a flange or leg, to clear another member or to let an angle bend round a corner
Mark the depth and width from the drawing
For a 90° bend in an angle frame, a 90° V is cut out of the leg on the inside of the corner, with its point at the heel

ul: **Square line round a pipe:** wrap a flexible strip (or a sheet of paper with a straight edge) tightly round the pipe so that its edge meets itself exactly, with no step. Scribe or soapstone along the edge.
**Lines along a pipe:** hold a straight edge along the pipe, or snap a chalk line along it, and mark the line.

**Quarter lines (0°, 90°, 180°, 270°):** measure the circumference with the strip or a tape (or work out π × outside diameter), divide by four, and step the quarters off round the pipe from a starting line. Label them and carry them along the pipe as far as you need.
**Centre of the pipe end:** use a centre head or a centre finder, or bisect two chords across the end.
Support pipe in vee blocks, or chock it, so it cannot roll while you mark or punch it.

blocks.note: A quick way to find the quarters: wrap a strip of paper round the pipe, cut it to the exact circumference, then fold it in half and in half again. The folds mark the quarters.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **template** is a full-size pattern of a part, used to mark out many identical parts quickly and the same every time, or to mark shapes that are hard to measure, such as the cut on the end of a pipe.

ul: Materials: thin sheet steel or aluminium for templates used many times; hardboard or plywood; heavy card or paper for pipe wraps and one-off jobs.
Make it accurately from the drawing, working from a datum edge with a square and rule, and include the hole centres.
Cut it out, file the edges smooth and straight, and drill small holes at the hole centres so that a scriber or punch can mark through them.
**Check it against the drawing** (every size, angle and hole position) and have the supervisor check it before it is used.
**Label it:** job number, part mark, quantity, material and thickness, date, and which side is up (and left or right hand).

flow: Lay the template on clean plate in the position that wastes least material
Clamp or hold it firmly
Mark round it with a scriber or soapstone, leaving room for the kerf between parts
Mark the hole centres through the template's holes
Check the first part against the drawing before marking the rest
Store the template flat and dry, where it will not be bent or used for anything else

blocks.p: A **development** is the flat shape that, when rolled, bent or folded, makes the finished part. It is also called the pattern or stretch-out. It is drawn full size on paper, card or straight onto the metal.

head: Method
Used for
The idea
rows: Parallel line development
Prisms and cylinders: pipe cut at an angle (mitres), square ducts, tee branches between pipes of the same size
Lines run parallel to the sides of the object; their lengths are carried across to a straight stretch-out
Radial line development
Cones, cone frustums, pyramids and hoppers whose sides meet at one point (the apex)
Lines radiate from the apex; the pattern is drawn with arcs centred on the apex
Triangulation
Transition pieces such as square-to-round, and shapes whose sides do not meet at one point
The surface is divided into triangles; the true length of each side is found and the triangles are laid out one by one

blocks.h: A 90° two-piece pipe mitre (parallel line development)

flow: Measure the pipe's outside diameter (OD)
Draw a side view of the pipe full size, with the cut line at 45° across it
Draw a half circle on the end of the side view and divide it into six equal parts (twelve round the whole pipe); number the points
Project lines from the points along the pipe to meet the 45° cut line
Beside the view, draw a straight stretch-out line π × OD long, divide it into twelve equal spaces, number them to match, and draw a line up from each point
Carry the height of each point on the cut line across to the matching line on the stretch-out
Join the points with a smooth curve and cut the template out
Mark the quarter lines on the pipe, wrap the template tightly with its ends meeting and lined up with the quarter lines, and mark round the curve; show the waste side

blocks.p: Use the **outside** diameter for a template that wraps round the outside of the pipe. Example: a pipe with an outside diameter of 76.1 mm needs a stretch-out of 3.142 × 76.1 ≈ 239 mm, divided into twelve spaces of about 19.9 mm.

blocks.note: Check your pattern: for a 45° cut, the highest point of the curve is one outside diameter above the lowest point. If the ends of the template overlap or leave a gap when wrapped, the stretch-out length is wrong.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Draw the front view: the base diameter, the top diameter and the height
Extend the two sloping sides until they meet at the apex
Draw a half plan of the base and divide it into six equal parts (twelve round the base)
With the apex as centre, draw a large arc whose radius is the slant length from the apex to the base
From the same centre, draw a smaller arc whose radius is the slant length from the apex to the top
Step off the twelve base divisions along the large arc
Join the first and last points to the apex; the pattern is the shape between the two arcs and these lines
Add any seam allowance, check, and cut out

blocks.p: The sloping side in the front view shows the true slant length. You can check the angle of the pattern by calculation: **angle = 360° × base radius ÷ slant length to the base**. Example: a frustum with a 600 mm base, a 200 mm top and a height of 400 mm. Its sides meet 600 mm above the base, the slant length to the base is √(300² + 600²) ≈ 670.8 mm, the slant length to the top is about 223.6 mm, and the angle of the pattern is 360 × 300 ÷ 670.8 ≈ 161°.

blocks.note: Draw developments with a sharp pencil and accurate instruments. Small errors in plotting add up to a large gap or overlap at the seam.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Allowances, checking and finishing the job

blocks.p: The drawing shows the **finished** size of each part. Cutting, bending, machining and welding all add or remove metal, so your marks must allow for them.

head: Allowance
Why it is needed
How it changes your marks
rows: Kerf

A cut removes a strip of metal. A hacksaw or band saw takes about 1–2 mm, an abrasive disc about 1–3 mm (depending on its thickness), and a plasma or oxy-fuel cut more, depending on the nozzle, the thickness and the settings.
Cut on the waste side of the line, so the line stays on the part
Or mark the cut line half a kerf into the waste
Leave a kerf's width between parts nested on one plate
Check the kerf on a test cut
Bending and rolling
When plate bends, the outside stretches and the inside squeezes; the middle of the thickness (the **neutral axis**) keeps its length
Work out flat lengths at the neutral axis
For a rolled cylinder, use the mean diameter
Mark bend lines from the flat length, not from the outside sizes
Machining or grinding
An edge to be machined or ground needs extra metal
Leave the extra the drawing or supervisor gives (often a few millimetres) and mark the cut line further out
Weld shrinkage
Welds shrink as they cool and pull parts shorter or closer together
Mark slightly long, or allow a gap, only as the drawing or supervisor says
Seams and laps
A lapped or folded seam needs extra metal
Add the allowance the drawing gives along the right edge of the pattern

blocks.p: **Mean diameter = inside diameter + thickness = outside diameter − thickness.** The length of plate to roll = π × mean diameter. Example: a shell with a 900 mm inside diameter from 8 mm plate has a mean diameter of 908 mm, so it needs 3.142 × 908 ≈ 2 853 mm of plate. Working from the inside diameter would make it about 25 mm short; from the outside diameter, about 25 mm long.

blocks.note: Tight bends in thick plate stretch differently. For those, the shop uses a bend allowance table or the press brake operator's figures; follow them.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Mark bend lines square to the datum, at the positions worked out from the flat length.
Mark the direction and angle of each bend (for example UP 90°) so the operator bends the right way.
Use a fine line, not a deep scratch, where the metal will bend.

flow: Stop before cutting
Check the drawing again: the revision, the quantity and the hand
Re-measure every size from the datums
Check the diagonals and the hole spacings
Check that the allowances are in and the waste side is marked
Ask the supervisor or a second person to check
Cut

ul: Paint the **part mark** and **job number** on each piece with a paint marker, where they will not be cut off, ground off or hidden by a weld.
Put them in the same place on every piece (for example near the datum end) so that the fitter finds them quickly.
Re-mark offcuts that go back to the rack with their material and size.

head: Problem
What to do
rows: A size is missing, or the sizes do not add up
Stop and ask the supervisor before you mark
The material is the wrong size, damaged or unlabelled
Set it aside and report it
A template does not match the drawing
Do not use it; report it
A tool is damaged: a bent tape hook, a dropped square
Take it out of use, label it and report it
You have marked something wrongly
Tell the supervisor, cross out the wrong marks clearly so nobody cuts to them, and re-mark

ul: Wipe the tools clean, oil steel tools lightly against rust, and cover sharp points.
Check tools for damage and report any faults.
Return every tool to its place, and cap marking fluids and paint markers.
Put offcuts in the right rack or bin and sweep the area.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can read a drawing and job card, check the revision and check that the sizes add up.
I can make or check a cutting list and plan cuts from stock lengths.
I can check material for size, straightness and damage.
I can lift, support and handle steel safely, and look after sharp tools.
I can choose the right tool and marker for the surface and the job, and keep my tools accurate.
I can choose and check datums and measure every size from them.
I can check squareness with diagonals and set out a right angle with the 3-4-5 rule.
I can bisect lines and angles, draw perpendicular and parallel lines, and find the centre of a circle or a bar.
I can work out a circumference, and the chord for holes equally spaced on a pitch circle.
I can mark holes from the pitch, end distance, edge distance and back mark, and punch them with witness marks.
I can carry a square line round a section and a pipe, and find the quarter lines on a pipe.
I can mark mitres, copes and notches and show the waste side.
I can make, check, label and use a template.
I can develop a pipe mitre by parallel lines and a cone frustum by radial lines.
I can allow for the kerf, bending, machining and weld shrinkage, and use the mean diameter for a rolled cylinder.
I can check a job before it is cut, mark part numbers, and report problems.

terms: Apex
The point at the top of a cone or pyramid where the sloping sides meet
Back mark
On an angle or channel flange, the distance from the back of the section to the line of holes; also called the gauge line
Bend line
A line marked across a plate to show where it will be bent
Centre line
A line of symmetry through the middle of a part or a hole
Centre punch
A punch with a point of about 90°, used to make the dent that starts a drill
Chalk line
A chalked string pulled tight and snapped to mark a long straight line
Chord
A straight line joining two points on a circle
Circumference
The distance all the way round a circle; π × diameter
Cope
A cut that shapes the end of a beam to fit round the flange of another beam
Cutting list
A list of every part with its section, size, length and quantity
Datum
The line, edge, face or point that all measurements are taken from
Development
The flat shape that rolls or folds into the finished part; also called the stretch-out or pattern
Dividers
A tool with two hardened points for small circles and stepping off equal distances
Dot (prick) punch
A punch with a fine point for light marks
Edge distance
From the side edge of a plate or flange to the centre of a hole
Framing square
A large flat steel square for marking and checking right angles on plate
End distance
From the end of a member to the centre of the first hole
Kerf
The width of metal removed by a cut
Marking blue
A quick-drying coating that makes scribed lines show clearly on bright metal
Mean diameter
The diameter at the middle of the plate thickness, used for rolled cylinders
Mitre
A joint where two members are cut at matching angles to meet at a corner
Paint marker
A pen filled with paint, for part marks that last on steel
Neutral axis
The line in the middle of a bent plate that neither stretches nor squeezes
Parallax
The error caused by reading a rule from an angle instead of straight on
Pitch
The centre-to-centre distance between holes in a line
Pitch circle diameter (PCD)
The diameter of the circle through the centres of a ring of holes
Plumb bob
A pointed weight on a string that hangs to show a true vertical line
Quarter lines
Lines at 0°, 90°, 180° and 270° round a pipe
Radial line development
Development of cones and pyramids with arcs drawn from the apex
Parallel line development
Development of prisms and cylinders, such as pipe mitres, with parallel lines
Scriber
A hardened pointed tool for scratching fine lines on metal
Soapstone
A soft stone (French chalk) used to mark rough or hot steel
Template
A full-size pattern used to mark identical parts
Trammels
A beam with two sliding points for large arcs and circles; a beam compass
Triangulation
Development of transition pieces by dividing the surface into triangles
UB, UC, PFC
Universal beam, universal column and parallel flange channel
RHS, SHS, CHS
Rectangular, square and circular hollow sections
Waste side
The side of a cut line that will be cut away, marked so that the kerf falls there
Witness marks
A circle or dots round a hole centre that show after drilling whether the hole is in place

c1.title: Column base plates for a school canteen in Black River
c1.text: Rushane works at a fabrication shop in Black River, St Elizabeth. He is marking out eight base plates for the steel columns of a new school canteen. Each plate is 12 mm mild steel, 350 mm × 250 mm, cut to size by the supplier. The drawing shows four Ø22 holes with their centres 45 mm in from each edge. The plates have patches of loose mill scale and light rust, and the holes will be drilled on a magnetic drill.

c2.title: A cover plate for a cistern in Christiana
c2.text: Shantel is marking out a round steel cover for a concrete water cistern at a guest house in Christiana, Manchester. The cover is 560 mm in diameter and will be cut from 6 mm plate with the plasma cutter. Twelve Ø12 holes for the fixing bolts must be equally spaced on a 480 mm pitch circle, to line up with bolts already set in the concrete. She has dividers, trammels, a steel rule, a calculator and marking blue.

c3.title: A mitred bend for a pump house near Lionel Town
c3.text: Damion is making a 90° two-piece mitred bend for the suction pipe of an irrigation pump house near Lionel Town, Clarendon. The steel pipe has an outside diameter of 114.3 mm and a 6 mm wall. He will develop a paper template by parallel lines, wrap it round the pipe, mark the cut with soapstone and cut it with oxy-fuel. The farm manager says a second, identical bend will be needed next month.

c4.title: Mezzanine steel for a shop in Half Way Tree
c4.text: Marlon is marking out steel for a storage mezzanine in a hardware shop in Half Way Tree, St Andrew. The floor beams are UB 203 × 133 × 25, each 4.8 m long, and each end bolts to a main beam through a 75 × 75 × 8 angle cleat. The drawing gives the cleat holes on a back mark of 45 mm.

c5.title: A tank shell and a hopper in Ewarton
c5.text: Nordia works at a small shop in Ewarton, St Catherine, that makes equipment for a feed mill. This week she must mark out a cylindrical tank shell, rolled from 6 mm plate, with an inside diameter of 1 000 mm. She must also develop the pattern for a hopper shaped like a cone with its top cut off: 800 mm across the base and 200 mm across the top. The drawing says the hopper's seam is lapped by 15 mm and welded.

questions.q: Before marking the holes, Rushane measures the diagonals of a plate: 430 mm and 436 mm. What does this tell him?
o: The corners are not square, so the edges cannot be trusted as datums
The plate is the right size, as cut plate always varies by about 6 mm
The plate is too small, because each diagonal should be about 600 mm
The plate is too thick for the holes and must go back to the supplier
questions.why: In a true rectangle both diagonals are equal (here √(350² + 250²) ≈ 430 mm). Unequal diagonals mean the corners are not 90°, so he checks the edges with a square and, if needed, scribes a square datum line to work from.

questions.q: How far apart should the hole centres be along the 350 mm length and across the 250 mm width?
o: 305 mm along and 205 mm across
260 mm along and 160 mm across
350 mm along and 250 mm across
395 mm along and 295 mm across
questions.why: Each hole is 45 mm in from both edges, so 2 × 45 = 90 mm comes off each size: 350 − 90 = 260 mm and 250 − 90 = 160 mm. He marks the lines at 45 mm and 305 mm, and at 45 mm and 205 mm, from the datum edges.

questions.q: How should Rushane prepare the plates so that his hole lines are fine and stay clear?
o: Draw the lines in soapstone straight over the scale and rust
Snap a chalk line across each plate for every hole line
Clean the hole areas to bright metal, blue them, then scribe
Mark the lines with a ballpoint pen straight onto the rusty surface
questions.why: Loose scale and rust flake off and take the marks with them. On cleaned metal, marking blue shows a fine scribed line clearly; soapstone lines are thick and suit rough work and flame-cut lines.

questions.q: The hole lines are scribed. In what order should Rushane mark the hole centres?
o: Centre punch each crossing hard, then check the spacing with a tape
Dot punch lightly, check, then centre punch and add witness marks
Drill small pilot holes at each crossing, then measure between them
Centre punch each crossing, then scribe the hole circles by eye
questions.why: A light dot can still be corrected if the check finds a mistake; a deep centre punch mark cannot, and it will pull the drill off line. The centre punch dent then guides the drill, and the witness marks show after drilling whether each hole is in place.

questions.q: What distance should Shantel set on her dividers to step off the twelve holes round the 480 mm pitch circle?
o: About 126 mm, the circumference divided by 12
About 40 mm, the pitch circle diameter divided by 12
About 240 mm, the radius of the pitch circle
About 124 mm, the chord for twelve equal holes
questions.why: Dividers measure the straight distance (chord) between holes: 480 × 0.259 ≈ 124 mm. The circumference divided by 12 (about 126 mm) is the arc round the curve; stepped off twelve times it would overshoot the start by about 17 mm.

questions.q: After stepping round the circle, Shantel's last step lands about 3 mm past her first mark. What should she do?
o: Close the dividers a fraction and step round again
Make the last gap 3 mm smaller than all the others
Move the first mark along by 3 mm and carry on
Accept it, as 3 mm is small on a large circle
questions.why: The 3 mm error is spread over twelve steps, so each step is about 0.25 mm too long. Correcting the dividers gives twelve equal gaps. Squeezing the error into one gap would leave a pair of holes that does not match the bolts in the concrete.

questions.q: How should Shantel mark the 560 mm outline that will be plasma cut, so that the line can still be followed and checked?
o: Draw it freehand in soapstone round a paint tin of the right size
Scribe it with trammels and punch dots evenly along the line
Mark it with a paint marker only, since punch dots weaken the plate
Snap four chalk lines to make a square and cut the corners off
questions.why: Trammels give a true circle from the centre. Punch dots along the line still show through the heat and slag of the cut, so the cutter can follow the line and anyone can check the cut afterwards.

questions.q: After drilling, the witness circle round one hole can be seen on one side only. What does this tell Shantel?
o: The hole has wandered away from the side where the mark shows
The hole is in the right place but was drilled a little oversize
The witness circle was scribed too small for this size of hole
The drill was blunt, but the hole itself is in the right place
questions.why: A hole drilled in the right place cuts through the witness circle evenly all round. If the mark has gone on one side and still shows on the other, the hole has moved towards the side where it has gone, and it must be checked against the bolts before the cover is fitted.

questions.q: What length should the stretch-out of Damion's paper template be?
o: About 340 mm, from the mean diameter
About 321 mm, from the inside diameter
About 359 mm, from the outside diameter
About 229 mm, twice the outside diameter
questions.why: The paper wraps round the outside of the pipe, so the stretch-out is π × outside diameter: 3.142 × 114.3 ≈ 359 mm. The mean diameter is used when plate is rolled into a cylinder, not for a wrap-round template.

questions.q: Why does Damion mark the quarter lines on the pipe before he wraps the template?
o: So the template lines up and the bend turns the right way
So that the soapstone line is easier to see on the dark pipe
So that he can measure the pipe's wall thickness at four points
So that the template does not need to be divided into equal parts
questions.why: The template's high and low points must sit on the pipe's quarter lines, which match the lines on the template. Then the cut is square to the pipe and the two pieces meet in the right plane, at 90°.

questions.q: Damion marks the cut line with soapstone. Where should the oxy-fuel cut be made?
o: Right down the centre of the soapstone line, to split it
On whichever side of the line the torch reaches more easily
On the part side, leaving metal to grind back later
Just on the waste side, so the line stays on the part
questions.why: The cut removes a strip of metal (the kerf). Cutting on the waste side keeps the marked line on the finished piece, so the pipe is not short and the mitre angle stays true.

questions.q: What should Damion do with the paper template after this job?
o: Throw it away, since a new one is quick to draw next month
Label it with the job, pipe size and angle; store it flat
Leave it wrapped on the pipe offcut in the yard until it is needed
Fold it small and keep it in his toolbox with the soapstone
questions.why: A labelled template, kept flat and dry, gives an identical bend next month with no new drawing. Damp, crumpled or unlabelled templates get used on the wrong pipe or give a poor fit; for many repeats, the shape can be transferred to thin sheet.

questions.q: What does the 25 in UB 203 × 133 × 25 tell Marlon?
o: The beam's flanges and web are each about 25 mm thick
The beam weighs about 25 kg for each metre of length
The beam is supplied in standard lengths of 25 feet
The bolt holes in the web must be 25 mm in diameter
questions.why: In a universal beam size, the figures are depth × flange width × mass per metre. The mass per metre lets you work out the weight of each length before you lift it.

questions.q: Marlon needs to move a 4.8 m floor beam onto the trestles. What is the safest plan?
o: Two people carry it on their shoulders, as it weighs about 50 kg
One person drags it by one end, as it is too long to carry
Use a lifting aid or enough people, as it weighs about 120 kg
Roll it along the floor on two lengths of pipe to the trestles
questions.why: 4.8 m × 25 kg/m ≈ 120 kg, far too heavy for two people to carry safely. Use a lifting aid, or enough people with one person giving the commands, and chock the beam on firm trestles.

questions.q: Where does Marlon measure the 45 mm back mark from on each cleat?
o: From the toe, the free edge of the leg
From the middle of the leg's width
From the end of the angle cleat
From the heel, the back of the angle
questions.why: The back mark is measured from the back (heel) of the angle across the leg. The toe is a rolled edge whose position varies, so measuring from it would put the hole line in the wrong place.

questions.q: What length of 6 mm plate should Nordia mark for the tank shell, before any allowance for the seam?
o: About 3 142 mm
About 3 160 mm
About 3 179 mm
About 3 123 mm
questions.why: When plate is rolled, the middle of its thickness keeps its length. Mean diameter = 1 000 + 6 = 1 006 mm, and π × 1 006 ≈ 3 160 mm. The inside diameter would make the shell about 19 mm short.

questions.q: When Nordia draws the front view of the hopper, why does she extend its two sloping sides until they meet?
o: To check that the hopper will be the right height overall
To find where the seam of the hopper should be welded
To work out what thickness of plate the hopper needs
To find the apex, the centre for the pattern's arcs
questions.why: In radial line development, the arcs of the pattern are drawn from the apex of the full cone, with radii equal to the slant lengths to the base and to the top.

questions.q: The drawing says the hopper's seam is lapped by 15 mm. What should Nordia do to her pattern?
o: Make both arcs 15 mm larger in radius
Add 15 mm to each of the curved edges
Add 15 mm along one straight edge for the lap
Nothing, as rolling stretches the plate enough
questions.why: The lap is an overlap where the two straight edges meet, so a 15 mm strip is added along one straight edge of the pattern. Making the arcs larger would change the height and diameters of the hopper.

questions.q: Kadeem must mark a line at 90° to the long edge of a 2.4 m × 1.2 m plate, 600 mm from one end. He has a tape, a chalk line and soapstone. Which method gives the most accurate right angle?
o: Measure 600 mm from the end along both long edges and join the marks
Line the chalk line up by eye with the end of the plate
Set out a 3-4-5 triangle with sides of 600, 800 and 1 000 mm
Use a small engineer's square and extend its line across the plate
questions.why: A large 3-4-5 triangle gives an accurate right angle from the edge itself. Measuring from the plate's end only works if the end is square, and a small square's error grows when its short line is extended across 1.2 m.

questions.q: Why should bend lines on aluminium or galvanised sheet be marked with a fine marker rather than a deep scribed line?
o: A scratch at the bend can start a crack and break the coating
Scribed lines cannot be seen on aluminium or galvanised sheet at all
The scriber point would be blunted by the zinc and the aluminium
Marker ink helps the sheet slide through the folding machine
questions.why: When metal bends, the outside of the bend stretches, and a scratch there can open into a crack. On galvanised sheet a scratch also breaks the zinc coating, which lets rust start.
